about: One entry per build of the web app, newest first. build = the number in the service worker cache name (docs/sw.js). Add an entry with every change; scripts/make_changelog.py writes CHANGELOG.md from this file.

releases.title: A diary of each day, for every computer
changes: Journal has a second tab, Diary: one row per day for the last 30 days with a score out of 100 and its stars, the time at the screen, the tasks asked of the assistants and how many finished, the assistants' working time, the processor and memory in use and the tokens

The score is worked out in the page from three parts: 35 for the screen time against 8 hours, 40 for the finished tasks against 200 and 25 for the assistants' time against 100 hours. A day with no screen time, no tasks and no tokens says Rest day instead of a zero

Each computer that syncs with the brain is found by itself, from the machine named on the session notes and from the notes in machines/. A row of chips picks all computers or one; nothing lists the computers by hand
A day opens to show each computer on its own: the hours it was in use, its load, and the log of the tasks asked that day, each one opening its session note

cairn vibe watch now notes the day's use of the computer it runs on in machines/<name>-activity.md, about every 30 minutes: minutes at the screen (a key or the mouse within the last 2 minutes), minutes awake, processor and memory average and peak, and the minutes in each hour. Windows and macOS; 120 days are kept; --no-laptop turns it off with the load note
The computer is looked at once a minute on a thread of its own, so a pass that takes minutes over a big brain does not lose the time in between
Not in this build: a computer's screen time and load start on the day its own Cairn has this build. Its earlier days show the tasks only. A phone has no watcher, so it has no row

releases.title: Video tiles show the video in Safari
changes: Repo pages: in Safari (so on an iPhone) the picture on a video’s tile was black since build 92. Safari says a frame is ready before it has one to give. A black picture is now taken again, a quarter of a second apart for up to three seconds, and a video that stays black gets no picture instead of a black one (#84)

releases.title: A repo opens with its Windows, Mac, iPhone and Android versions
changes: The Look tab of a repo starts with Versions: four lines, Windows, Mac, iPhone and Android, each with the file to download or the words "not published". The Releases tab lists every release with its files; this answers whether the project can be had on your computer and your phone (#83)

Windows, Mac and Android are read from the releases, the newest release that has a file for them, with its size and age. A download the README links counts too, such as an install script kept on the project's own site (#83)

iPhone is the project's own web app on the home screen: the repo holds a web manifest that opens as its own app and its page has an apple-touch-icon. The line links the live app and says how to add it; when one of the two is missing it says which (#83)
A version that an older release still carries while newer releases dropped it is marked as left behind, with the release that passed it (#83)

In a repo of many apps each app's folder shows its own four, from the releases whose tag starts with the folder's name. The repo's own page says how many apps the releases belong to instead of mixing them (#83)
One look costs one more GitHub call, kept for five minutes. Not in this build: whether a version starts was not looked at, only whether it is published

releases.title: Issues, pull requests, releases and branches inside Cairn
changes: Repo pages have two more tabs. Releases shows each release with its notes and its files to download. Issues and pull requests lists the open ones, with the closed ones one press away; one opens with everything said on it, and a pull request also shows its reviews, the comments left on lines and the files it changes (#81)
Branches: the branch name under a repo’s title lists its branches. Picking one shows that branch’s pictures, README, pushes and files, and every step from there stays on it (#81)

A link to github.com anywhere in Cairn (a note, Vibe, Home, a README, the version history) now opens that repo, folder, file, push, pull request, issue or list of releases inside Cairn. Ctrl or Cmd with the click still opens github.com, and so does every button that says GitHub. Downloads, and pages Cairn has no place for, stay on GitHub (#81)
Pictures and videos: up to six videos lead the grid, so a folder of many covers no longer pushes every video off the first screen, and Pictures or Videos can be shown alone (#81)
A video’s tile is now a picture taken from the video instead of a live player. A phone gives a page only a few video players, and a grid of videos could use them up before the one you opened (#81)
A video this browser cannot play (a phone’s own recording opened in another browser, say) now says so and offers to save it, instead of showing an empty box (#81)

One thing a browser cannot do: save a file of a private repo’s release without github.com. GitHub refuses that request from any web page, so those files download through github.com and the page says so (#81)

releases.title: Your AI app remembers from the cloud when the brain is not on the computer
changes: The memory Cairn gives your AI app no longer depends on the brain's folder being on the computer. A brain that is pushed to GitHub is read from there when the folder is missing: a new computer, a wiped disk, a folder that was moved. The chat is told in the first line that the answer comes from GitHub

Something to remember is then saved on GitHub itself, and every device's Cairn picks it up at its next sync. It never replaces a note that is there, keeps a computer's own folder (--write-folder), and still refuses text that looks like a password, key or token

cairn connect vector --cloud owner/repo connects a computer that never had the brain's folder. No clone and no Cairn open: the text of the notes is fetched once (about 20 MB and half a minute for 4,500 notes), then only what changed (a second or two)
Add --cloud to a search or a save to use the newest notes on GitHub on purpose, for when Cairn on this computer has not synced yet
It works even when Cairn's own code is gone from the computer (Python 3.9 or newer, nothing to install), and without a connection the last fetched notes still answer, with their age said

It needs a GitHub sign-in on the computer (gh auth login, or the one git already uses). GitHub cannot search inside a private repo's notes, which is why their text is fetched; pictures and other files are not

releases.title: Messages between computers leave at once, and a phone takes part
changes: A message for another computer leaves the moment it is written, where the brain syncs by itself: the desktop app with automatic sync on, or a brain whose repository names a sync command (git config cairn.sync). While the app is open it asks the remote every 20 seconds whether something new is there, so the other computer's message shows on Today without a reload. Before, a message waited for the next round, up to 10 minutes (#79)

From a terminal the same: cairn handoff send and an answer say whether they were sent now, and cairn handoff fetches before it lists. Without the setting nothing is pushed for you and the command says the message goes with the next sync (#79)

A phone and the web app take part. They go by a name kept in that browser (Phone until you press Rename), a message can be for that name, and they pick up, finish and close like a computer. Before, they could only read and answer (#79)
Close for everyone: any device can call a conversation off for all of them, in the app and with cairn handoff close (#79)

The order no longer depends on the clocks. A message carries the same moment in UTC and names the message it follows, so two time zones read the same order and an answer never shows before what it answers (#79)

Assistants reach it without a terminal: cairn mcp has handoffs, handoff_send and handoff_answer, and the memory skill that Cairn puts into your AI app looks at what another computer left when a chat starts (#79)
Pages open on a computer now show notes that arrived through a sync made outside Cairn (a script, a pull in a terminal) within seconds (#79)

releases.title: Found on Google by what it does, not only by its name
changes: Cairn in search results: the title and description now say what Cairn is in the words people type when they have never heard of it (open-source second brain, Markdown, Git repo, task board, decision log, journal), and the description search engines read lists the same

Public brain page: a note with a claim is titled by the claim in search results, for example “Built titip: Outlook inbox from a paired phone” instead of “titip”. The heading on the page stays the note’s own title ([#77](https://github.com/juw12/cairn/pull/77))

Public brain page: the first page’s title says what it is and how much is on it, and every page describes itself in the form search engines read: what it is, who wrote it, when it last changed, its tags and the links that back it ([#77](https://github.com/juw12/cairn/pull/77))

releases.title: Your AI app remembers, with nothing to set up
changes: A new chat in Vector now starts with your brain as its memory on every computer that has Cairn. Each time Cairn opens it puts a small skill, cairn-memory, where Vector reads skills: search the brain before answering, and save what the next chat will need. Nothing to run and nothing to set up (#71)

cairn connect does the same for Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex when you name them (cairn connect claude). They are not connected by themselves, because they also run unattended jobs. cairn connect --status shows what is connected, --remove takes it out, --off stops the automatic part (#71)
On a brain shared by several computers, cairn connect --write-folder devices/laptop makes this computer save its memory only in its own folder, so two computers never write the same note (#71)

Cairn leaves alone what is not its own: an app that is not installed gets no folder, a cairn-memory skill you wrote yourself is never touched, and opening a second brain does not move the skill away from the first (#71)
Saving refuses text that looks like a password, key or token, never overwrites a note, and says after each save whether the brain's copy on its git remote is up to date (#71)
The skill's two scripts leave no extra files in the app's skills folder, and the check after a save no longer depends on how git spells the path

releases.title: Your computers leave messages for each other
changes: Today has a new block, Between computers: a conversation between the computers that share one brain. One leaves a message for one, several or all of the others (what it found, what is left hanging, what only another computer can do); the others press Picked up, answer, and press Done (#75)

What waits for this computer is listed first, then what it is waiting for, then what is between other computers. A conversation is settled when every computer it was for has said Done, or when the one that started it closes it (#75)

From a terminal or an assistant: cairn handoff shows what was left for this computer; cairn handoff send "..." --to "<computer>" leaves a message (a few words of the name are enough, --to all is every computer); pickup, done, reply and show work on one conversation (#75)

Every message is its own file in handoffs/, written once by the computer that says it and never changed, so two computers never write the same file and the brain's sync has nothing to merge. On the web app and a phone you can read every conversation and answer (#75)
The agent instructions on the Vibe page name the two commands, so an assistant looks for what was left for its computer before it starts (#75)

releases.title: Your public brain is a web page anyone can search
changes: Public brain: the notes you mark publish: true now also go online as a web page, at https://your-name.github.io/brain/. Anyone can read it without Cairn, a GitHub account or a sign-in. Publishing puts the page in the docs folder of your public repo in the same commit and switches GitHub Pages on for it ([#73](https://github.com/juw12/cairn/pull/73))

The page has a search box over every public note. Every word you type must be in the note; a word in the title counts most, then a tag, then the text. / jumps to the box and the address keeps the search, so a search can be sent as a link ([#73](https://github.com/juw12/cairn/pull/73))

Google and Bing can find the notes: each one is its own page with a title, a description and its own address, and a sitemap lists them all with the day each last changed ([#73](https://github.com/juw12/cairn/pull/73))

Settings, Public brain: under Publish now there is a link to the page once it is online. Until then the line says what is missing, for instance the one GitHub setting only the owner of the repo can turn on

Each computer publishes once more by itself after this update, so the page appears without anyone asking. A repo that keeps something else in its docs folder is left alone ([#73](https://github.com/juw12/cairn/pull/73))

Cairn itself is easier to find: the app names one address for search engines whatever follows the question mark, says what it is in the form they read, has its own sitemap, and shows a short description with links when JavaScript is off

releases.title: Look inside a repo without opening GitHub
changes: Projects: a repo’s name now opens the repo inside Cairn instead of on github.com. The Look tab shows every picture and video in it, the most telling first (banners, screenshots and demos before app icons), its folders as cards with a cover picture, and its README as GitHub draws it (#72)
Any folder opens the same way, so a repo that holds many projects (one folder each) can be walked project by project, each with its own pictures, videos and README (#72)
A picture or video opens full screen. Arrow keys, the two buttons or a swipe step through the rest, and the name under it opens the file (#72)

Pushes tab: the latest 30 commits that touched the repo or the folder. A commit opens to its full message, the pictures and videos it brought as they were in that commit, the files it changed and the changed lines (#72)
Files tab: the folder’s listing. A file opens as a picture, a video, sound, rendered Markdown or plain text, with a Download button (#72)

Private repos work when you are signed in as someone who can read them: their files are fetched with your sign-in and never asked of GitHub’s public file host. Videos are fetched the same way for every repo, because that host sends them as a download and a phone would not play them (#72)

The place is in the address (#/projects/owner/repo/tab/folder), so Back goes up one step, a reload stays put and a link can be kept. Typing owner/repo in the Projects box opens that repo. One look costs three GitHub requests, and the file list is only asked again after a new push (#72)

Nothing in a README can run or restyle Cairn: only known tags and attributes are kept, and its links to the web open in a new tab. Each card keeps a GitHub link for the day you do want github.com (#72)

releases.title: Recap reads right on a phone
changes: Recap on Board, Ideas, Decisions, Notes, Map and Autopilot: on a brain read from GitHub (the phone) every row was squeezed into the narrow time column, one word a line. A row now uses its whole width, shows the note’s own day (today, yesterday, Nov 12) and the list is in that order, newest first (#69)
The “changed this week” number on Board, Ideas, Decisions and Notes counts by the same dates, so on the phone it no longer says 0 above a list of today’s changes (#69)
Recap: a title that is a whole paragraph is shortened to about three lines; the note itself keeps the full title (#69)

Code inbox on the phone no longer says “Scanning your code…” for ever. It says there is no code to scan there, and its Recap lists only tasks made from a code comment, not every note that was synced from somewhere (#69)
Journal, On your mind: a long name in a chip is shortened with dots and keeps its count, instead of being cut at the edge of the card (#69)
Autopilot queue on a phone shows two lines of each title instead of about twenty characters (#69)
Chat shows an older chat’s day as “Nov 12”, not “11/12/2026”. Canvas Recap shows how many cards a canvas has when its edit time is not known (#69)

releases.title: Built-in plugins set themselves up on every device
changes: Plugins: a plugin that comes with Cairn now installs itself on each of your devices when the brain's plugin list names it, so one list sets up your computer, laptop and phone. Before, every device had to be asked (#68)
This happens only in a brain you can edit, and never on a device where you turned plugins off. A plugin from outside Cairn still asks before it installs (#68)
The plugin list is found whether its folder is cairn or Cairn, as a vault kept on Windows or macOS may name it (#68)

releases.title: Pocket meter plugin
changes: Plugins: a new built-in plugin, Pocket meter. It draws a bar from zero to your ceiling from one note in your brain: the filled part is money that has arrived, a marker shows what is expected, a band shows the likely range, and a list shows which sources contribute (#67)
The plugin holds no figures. They live in a note you mark with pocket-meter: true, so they stay as private as that note. With no such note, the page shows the properties to add (#67)

releases.title: Private pictures open directly
changes: Latest updates uses the vault’s known paths to load a private picture without asking GitHub for a file that isn’t there. A picture beside the note still wins when both folders contain it (#66)
A phone-sized WebKit test now opens the Map with 4,000 notes and checks that it draws the linked notes and responds to a tap (#66)

releases.title: Map opens on a big brain
changes: Map and a note's Unlinked mentions no longer freeze on a large brain. On 4,000 notes the search for mentions took 5 seconds in Chrome and did not finish in Safari on a phone; it takes half a second in both now, with the same results (#64)
Home: the first line of an update is no longer the name of its picture when the note starts with one (#64)
Home: a note named for a time of day that has not come yet no longer sits on top of Latest updates. It keeps its day and shows no time (#64)

releases.title: A Home that shows what matters
changes: Home leads with what waits for you: sessions that stopped on an error, GitHub minutes running low, the newest tasks marked needs-me and decisions that wait for a yes or no (#62)
Home: Working now lists the running sessions with their computer, assistant, last step and tokens. The numbers are today's: working now, shipped, sessions, tokens, waiting for you, open tasks (#62)
Home: an activity chart you can tap or drag across. Sessions, shipped, tokens or journal lines per day over 14, 30 or 90 days, and under it what happened on the day you picked (#62)
Home: Latest updates shows your dated notes with a first line and a picture, from the note itself or from the project it names. A run of automatic notes folds into one row (#62)
Home: Computers shows every computer that writes into the brain, what runs there and when it was last heard (#62)
Phone: recap rows no longer run into each other on Home, Board, Ideas, Decisions and Notes. Long task titles and the Autopilot tiles no longer push the page sideways on a small phone (#62)
Pictures in a private brain on GitHub now load on the phone when you are signed in (#62)

releases.title: Dashboards has its own icon
changes: Dashboards on phone: the page has its own icon (four tiles on paper) on the Home Screen, in the tab and in its bar, so it no longer looks like Cairn. The mark in the bar is no longer a link to Cairn's home. Dashboards are still set up and signed in from Cairn as before (#60)

releases.title: Your totals across computers
changes: People: your row on the leaderboard counts every computer that syncs into the brain, says so, and lets you pick which computers count. What you publish follows the same choice (#58)
People: an unpublished row now reads "not published" instead of "only on this device", which sounded as if only one computer was counted (#58)

releases.title: Who pushes, on the folded GitHub block
changes: Vibe: folded, the GitHub minutes block still says which account this computer pushes as, next to the percent used (#56)

releases.title: Which GitHub account this computer pushes as
changes: Vibe: where the GitHub CLI is signed in to several accounts, a chip per account under the GitHub meters picks the one this computer pushes as. git, the GitHub CLI and an assistant working there all follow it, and a switch made in a terminal shows on the page (#55)
cairn vibe github push-as says which account pushes, and with a name switches to it (#55)

releases.title: GitHub minutes of a second account
changes: Vibe: a meter of GitHub Actions minutes for every account you are signed in to, not only the main one. Name the others with cairn vibe watch --github-account NAME (#53)
Vibe: hand a private repo to another of your accounts from the meter, so its minutes count there. GitHub mails the new owner to confirm, and the old owner keeps push access (#53)

releases.title: Dashboard buttons from the phone
changes: Dashboards on phone: a dashboard's buttons can run on your PC. Each press runs once, is refused when it is older than 5 minutes, and is taken back when the PC does not pick it up (#51)
Dashboards on phone: the open tab and folded blocks of a dashboard stay as they were when a newer copy arrives (#51)

releases.title: Version history
changes: Version history inside the app: every build with its date and what changed. Open it at the bottom of the sidebar, from Settings or from the command palette (#50)

releases.title: Journal per day, several computers
changes: Journal: one line per day, mood worked out for you, any period, and its own sidebar entry (#48)
Vibe: several computers in one brain with a device switch; a Mac can run the watcher (#49)
Every remaining page is made of blocks with a dashboard and a recap (#47)

releases.title: Blocks you fold and arrange
changes: Vibe blocks you fold and arrange, shared through the brain; the sidebar goes from 9 entries to 6; Founder Studio leaves Cairn (#45)
Vibe: a session works or is finished, never waits; one live list; Projects, People and Proof as blocks; 5 sidebar entries (#46)

releases.title: Smooth phone map, public page
changes: The phone map stays smooth on a big brain, a Telegram bot reports Cairn's status daily, UI tidy (#43)
A public page you can host anywhere: cairn publish --site (#44)

releases.title: Faster Vibe, GitHub minutes
changes: Vibe shows the computer (CPU, memory, power, time since restart) and effort follows its real load
The Vibe page never waits on git or on the computer reading, and no longer re-reads every note per poll
GitHub Actions minutes against the free limit, with a warning near it and a history
Autopilot: a lost connection no longer blocks a job, it waits and tries again
Desktop: updates apply even when git is slow; chat opens without waiting for the model list
Phone: any-network sign-in opens on Vibe, the app reloads into new versions, a GitHub brain loads every session
Plugin catalogue: Kilat 0.2.3 (#42)

releases.title: Tokens, models and sharing
changes: The Vibe watcher reads OpenCode 2.2: model, effort, tokens and turn state
Vibe stats: tokens, usage per model, prompts, active days and streak
A live recap band; continue an OpenCode session or start a chat in its folder from the recap
A share card for the last 14 days (story and square picture)
People: friends and a leaderboard from totals you choose to share

releases.title: Dashboards on the phone, MCP Registry
changes: Dashboards on the phone: cairn dashboards publishes local dashboard pages to the private relay repo, on a schedule
The home-screen app opens your brain signed in, with live sync for brains opened from GitHub
A Cairn tile for the iPhone widget (#41)
Published to the official MCP Registry as a bundle; every MCP tool declares its hints
Plugin catalogue: Kilat 0.2.2 (#40)

releases.title: Sign in by QR, several PCs on one relay
changes: Sign in a phone by QR code from Settings, on any network
Several PCs on one relay: the phone picks which one to talk to
Signed-in browsers reopen the last brain, so phone, laptop and PC show the same Map and Live
Big vaults open fast (notes fetched 100 per call), with a loading message while a brain opens
Plugins: Kilat, calculations with units, joins the catalogue (#35, #36)
Minimum Python is 3.13 (#38)

releases.title: Phone and chat
changes: Pair a phone by QR code to watch Cairn from it
Phone access from any network through Tailscale
Live sync between phone and PC
Chat with your OpenCode models from any device, also through a private GitHub relay repo
A live progress bar, time left and effort for running sessions

releases.title: Hubs, projects and databases
changes: Sidebar: 17 entries become 8 hubs with tabs inside the page (#30)
Projects ranking, Notion-style databases and a / menu (#31)
Vibe: an overview band with every status at a glance and what is running now (#32)
Founder Studio follows Cairn's controls and theme (#28, #29, #33)
The local server still answers when the git check stalls (#34)

releases.title: MCP, precedent and autopilot
changes: cairn mcp connects AI assistants, and stays fast on vaults of 2,000 notes (#17)
Precedent and autopilot inside Cairn (#19, #23)
Vibe: honest numbers at 286 sessions, 'code changed' for detected sessions, tap a figure to have it explained (#18, #21, #22)
Phones: the Log button sits in thumb reach and tucks away while you read (#24)
Founder Studio page: run the buyer panel inside Cairn (#26, #27)

releases.title: Sessions found on their own, offline voice
changes: Vibe finds OpenCode and Vector sessions by itself (#12)
Voice log: offline voice on the device, recall of any day, voice search, a 12-month heatmap (#13)
Vibe: clock-time totals, commit evidence, history grouped by day (#14)
Vibe: outcome filters, days that fold, and the desktop app runs the watcher (#15)
Voice log: monthly review, reviews that are due, days that read alike (#16)

releases.title: Obsidian, canvas, voice log and Vibe
changes: Obsidian import and two-way sync, and a live interactive map (#1)
Proof of work page and a design pass (#2)
Obsidian parity: callouts, embeds, split view, link suggestions, rename, properties, folders, templates, a first-run tour (#3)
The desktop app updates itself, no restarts by hand (#4)
Sync through office proxies, auto-publish of the public brain, maths and diagrams (#5)
Canvas, tabs and community plugins (#6, #9)
Voice daily log: mic button, spoken commands, 'Hey Cairn', languages, @people (#10, #11)
Vibe: live AI coding sessions, results, stats, feedback and skill runs (#8)

releases.title: Desktop app and the map
changes: Desktop app for Windows: one-click installer, tray icon, sync, open and settings inside the app
Map: filters, local maps, paths, suggested links, keyboard navigation; opens Obsidian vaults as they are
The map in 2D or 3D
Continue with GitHub sign-in
Design pass: map labels never overlap, 320 px phones fit

releases.title: First release
changes: Cairn 1.0: a second brain that lives inside your repo
People: explore GitHub profiles and read-only brains
Sign in with GitHub and edit your brain from any device
